stem: A client has a minor acute ankle sprain with swelling. Which home-care instruction about cold therapy is appropriate?

options.A: Apply a heating pad immediately after the sprain because early heat reliably decreases inflammation and limits acute swelling.
options.B: Use a cold pack wrapped in a towel for short applications, such as about 20 minutes at a time, during the acute phase of the sprain.
options.C: Place ice directly on bare skin for prolonged applications because longer contact improves pain relief without increasing tissue risk.
options.D: Avoid cold therapy during the first day because early swelling should be encouraged to increase blood flow to the injured ligament.

rationale: NIAMS recommends ice for minor acute sports injuries to reduce pain and inflammation. It advises applying an ice pack for about 20 minutes at a time, using a towel barrier, and avoiding more than 20 minutes to reduce cold-injury risk. NIAMS also cautions that heat should not be used immediately after an injury because it can increase inflammation and swelling. B is correct.
educational_objective: Use wrapped cold therapy for about 20 minutes at a time during the acute phase of a minor sprain and avoid direct prolonged ice contact or immediate heat.
source_organization: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS), NIH
source_document_title: Sports Injuries: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Steps to Take
source_locator: Treatment of Minor Injuries > R-I-C-E > Ice: apply ice pack 20 minutes at a time four to eight times daily; wrap cold pack/ice in a towel; do not exceed 20 minutes. Heat caution: do not use heat immediately after injury because it tends to increase inflammation and swelling.
source_claim_supported: For a minor acute sprain, wrapped cold therapy for about 20 minutes at a time is appropriate; prolonged direct ice contact and immediate heat should be avoided.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort, printed p.11: provide nonpharmacological comfort measures, assess/intervene for pain, apply/manage orthopedic devices and promote circulation.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because immediate heat can increase inflammation/swelling.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because prolonged direct ice exposure increases cold-injury risk.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because ice is recommended in the acute phase rather than avoided to encourage swelling.
